stem: An analytics team stores its reporting datasets in the BigQuery `US` multi-region. The DR requirement for a regional outage is an RPO of 4 hours and an RTO of 24 hours. The team lead says that no DR work is needed, because a multi-region location already replicates data across regions. What should the architect recommend?

options.text: Accept the current design, because the `US` multi-region keeps copies of the data in several US regions.
Replicate the datasets to a second region, because the `US` multi-region stores the data in a single region.
Rely on BigQuery time travel, because it can restore any table to a point in time within the last 7 days.
Move the datasets to a single US region, because regional datasets replicate synchronously to a second region.

explanation: The team lead's assumption is wrong. In BigQuery, a multi-region location does not provide cross-region replication, and the data is stored in a single region within the location. To survive a regional outage, replicate the data to another region. Cross-region dataset replication copies the data continuously, which meets the 4-hour RPO. The secondary replica is read-only, and you cannot promote it during a total outage of the primary region. If the team must also write during the outage, use managed disaster recovery (Enterprise Plus edition). It provisions slots in the second region and controls failover. Do not choose a region within the scope of the multi-region, such as `us-central1` for `US`, because Google warns of correlated failure.

whyWrong.A: A BigQuery multi-region stores the data in two zones of a single region. A regional outage makes it unavailable.
whyWrong.C: Time travel helps with corruption or deletion, but the data stays in the same location. It does not protect against a regional outage.
whyWrong.D: A regional dataset is stored in two zones of that region. It has no cross-region copy.

stem: A retailer runs its production e-commerce platform on Google Cloud. After a costly outage, leadership sets two support requirements: a first response within 15 minutes for critical production cases, and an assigned Google technical contact who learns the company's architecture and gives proactive guidance. Open a second case at priority P1 for the same issue, so that it gets a faster response.
Ask your Technical Account Manager to raise the priority of the case.
Change the case priority to P1, and describe how the business impact has changed.

explanation: The issue makes the service unusable in production with critical business impact, so it meets the P1 definition. You can increase an existing P2 to P4 case to P1 when production is affected, and you describe how the business impact changed. For a high-impact issue, the correct priority, not an escalation, gets the fast response.

stem: An on-call engineer sees connection errors from a Cloud SQL instance in one zone. The public Google Cloud Service Health page at status.cloud.google.com shows no incidents. The engineer must find out quickly if a Google Cloud incident affects the project. What should the engineer do?

Conclude that no Google Cloud incident exists, because the public page lists all confirmed incidents.
Subscribe to the RSS feed of the public Google Cloud Service Health page, and wait for an update.
Open a P4 support case, and ask Customer Care to confirm whether an incident exists.

explanation: Google communicates limited-scope incidents, such as incidents in a single zone or location, only through Personalized Service Health. The public page shows broad, severe incidents. Personalized Service Health is the primary source for disruptions that are relevant to your projects.

whyWrong.B: The public page shows broad, severe incidents. An incident in one zone can appear only in Personalized Service Health.

stem: A company runs production workloads in 30 projects. The SRE team wants Google Cloud incident information in its incident response process. On-call engineers must not get a page for every Google Cloud event. The process must also work during a widespread disruption that makes Personalized Service Health unavailable. Which two actions should you take? (Choose two.)

options.text: Show Personalized Service Health incidents on the team's dashboards, and send alerts only for events with a relevance of Related or Impacted.
Page the on-call engineer for every new Personalized Service Health event in every product and location, so that no Google Cloud incident is missed.
Use the public Google Cloud Service Health page as the primary source of incident data, because it needs no sign-in and has an RSS feed.

Add a runbook step that sends operators to status.cloud.google.com, and make automation use the public RSS feed when the Status API resource of the Service Health API reports Personalized Service Health issues.
Create a P1 support case automatically for each new Personalized Service Health event, so that Customer Care engages at once.

explanation: Google recommends that you show Personalized Service Health incidents on dashboards instead of paging for every event, and that you filter alerts to critical services or to Related and Impacted events. Personalized Service Health depends on core services such as IAM. The fallback for operators is the public page. For automation, the Status API resource of the Service Health API detects a Personalized Service Health problem, and the systems then read the public RSS feed.

whyWrong.B: A page for every event causes alert fatigue. Google recommends dashboards and filtered alerts instead.
whyWrong.C: The public page shows only broad, severe incidents. Personalized Service Health is the primary source, and the public page is the fallback.
whyWrong.E: A P1 case is for critical impact on your production. Automatic cases for known Google incidents only duplicate the known issue, and Customer Care asks you to review known issues before you create a case.

stem: During a major outage, engineers from three teams change production settings at the same time, and some changes undo others. Executives also call the engineers directly to ask for status. The engineer who declared the incident acts as the incident commander. What should the incident commander do next?

options.text: Take over all debugging personally, so that one person controls every production change and every status update.
Let each team change its own components, and ask each team to post its status in the incident document.
Assign an operations lead whose team is the only group that changes production, and a communications lead who sends periodic updates to stakeholders.
Stop all changes to production until a postmortem finds the root cause of the outage and the correct fix.

explanation: The problems are uncoordinated changes and interruptions. Google's incident roles solve both. The operations team is the only group that modifies the system, and the communications lead is the public face of the response and sends periodic updates. The incident commander keeps the high-level state and delegates.

whyWrong.A: The incident commander holds the high-level state and delegates work. If the commander also debugs, nobody coordinates the response.
whyWrong.B: Parallel changes by several teams cause the conflicts in the stem. Only the operations team should change the system during an incident.
whyWrong.D: Incident response puts mitigation first: stop the bleeding and restore service. The postmortem comes after the incident.

stem: A product team ships new features every day. The service missed its availability SLO in each of the last three months, and the SREs spend most of their time on incidents. The product manager says that features are the priority, and the SREs want to stop releases. Each release decision becomes an argument. What should you recommend?

options.text: Require a change advisory board to approve every release until the service meets its SLO for a full quarter.
Write an error budget policy that the product manager, the developers, and the SREs approve, which stops non-critical releases when the error budget is spent.
Raise the SLO target, so that the developers see a larger gap between the target and the measured availability.
Let the SRE team decide alone which releases to block, based on its judgment of the risk of each change.

explanation: The problem is a repeated conflict about release decisions. The error budget is an objective metric, and a written error budget policy states the actions to take when the budget is spent and who takes them. The product manager, the development team, and the SREs must all approve the policy, so the decision is agreed before the next release.

whyWrong.A: DORA research recommends peer review instead of heavyweight change-approval processes. A board adds delay and does not create an agreed reliability rule.
whyWrong.C: A higher target only makes the error budget smaller. Without an agreed policy, nothing changes when the service misses the target.
whyWrong.D: A decision by one team brings back the politics that the error budget removes. All key stakeholders must approve the policy.

stem: A team deploys a containerized service once a month. A weekly change advisory board (CAB) meeting approves each release. A separate team scans the container images for vulnerabilities after the images reach production. Releases often cause incidents, and the lead time for changes is long. Leadership wants fewer failed changes and faster delivery. Which two changes should you recommend? (Choose two.)

options.text: Add a second CAB review for each change that the first CAB marks as high risk.
Combine the monthly releases into quarterly releases, so that each release gets more testing.
Replace the CAB with peer code review and automated tests that run on every pull request.
Set `allowFailure: true` on the test steps in Cloud Build, so that flaky tests do not block releases.
Add On-Demand Scanning to the Cloud Build pipeline, and block the build when an image has vulnerabilities at or above a set severity.

explanation: DORA research recommends peer review instead of heavyweight change approval, and automated tests on each pull request catch defects before merge. On-Demand Scanning in the Cloud Build pipeline moves the vulnerability check before deployment, and the build stops when the severity matches the threshold. Both changes improve stability without slowing delivery.

whyWrong.A: More approval steps add delay. DORA recommends peer review instead of heavyweight change-approval processes.
whyWrong.B: Bigger batches increase lead time and delay feedback. DORA recommends small batches for shorter lead times and faster feedback.
whyWrong.D: With `allowFailure: true`, the build succeeds even when the test step fails, so the tests stop being a quality gate.

stem: A CTO wants to compare the software delivery performance of 12 product teams with industry research. The measures must cover both the speed and the stability of software changes. Which metrics should the teams report?

stem: A payments service had three similar outages this quarter. Each outage used more than 20% of the four-week error budget. Each postmortem produced action items with one owner and a tracking bug, but most items are still open because the team always gives feature work a higher priority. The team's error budget policy covers only SLO misses. What should you recommend?

options.text: Add an outage rule to the error budget policy: an incident that uses over 20% of the four-week budget needs a P0 action item. Track closure.
Reward engineers based on the number of postmortems that they write and publish each quarter, so that postmortems get more attention.
Assign each action item to several owners from different teams, so that more people can work on it at the same time.
Replace the open action items with one broad item, "Improve the reliability of the payments service", and give it to the team lead.

explanation: The action items exist and are tracked, but feature work always wins. The SRE workbook example policy says that an incident that uses more than 20% of the four-week budget needs a postmortem with at least one P0 action item for the root cause. A P0 item goes before feature work, and monitoring the closure of action items shows when items slip.

whyWrong.B: If you reward the writing of postmortems but not the closure of action items, you get unclosed postmortems.
whyWrong.C: The workbook recommends a single owner with several collaborators. Several owners weaken accountability.
whyWrong.D: Action items need a verifiable end state. A broad item such as "improve reliability" cannot be measured or closed.

stem: A retail company runs its checkout app on Compute Engine and Cloud Run in its own Google Cloud projects. The security team hired an outside firm to run a penetration test against the app next week. The CISO asks what the company must do with respect to Google before the test starts. stem: A company runs a customer portal on App Engine. Signed-in users can post public comments and change their email settings. Before a major release, the security team wants Web Security Scanner to crawl the signed-in pages and find cross-site scripting issues. The scan must not change production data or send email to real customers. What should you do?

Use the weekly managed scans in production, because they crawl the signed-in pages without submitting any forms.
Run a custom scan against production with an administrator account, so that the scanner can reach every page.
Run a custom scan against production at night, and delete the test comments and test emails after the scan.

Use a test account that has no access to sensitive data or harmful operations. A custom scan can also sign in to the app, which the signed-in pages need.

stem: A logistics company runs its dispatch app on 40 Compute Engine VMs in `us-east4`. Its DR plan fails over to `us-central1`, where the project has enough quota for 40 VMs of the same machine type. During the last failover drill, VM creation failed in two zones because those zones had no capacity for that machine type. The business requires high assurance that the DR VMs can start during a real failover. What should you do?

options.text: Request a quota increase for the machine type in `us-central1`, so that the project can create more VMs than it needs.
Buy a three-year compute flexible committed use discount for `us-central1` to secure the capacity for the DR VMs.
Create a regional MIG in `us-central1` that autoscales from 0 to 40 VMs, and configure autohealing for it.
Create Compute Engine reservations for the needed VMs in the `us-central1` zones that the DR plan uses.

explanation: The drill failed because the zones had no capacity, not because of quota. A quota sets the maximum number of resources that you can create, but it does not guarantee that the resources are available. A reservation gives a high level of assurance of capacity for the VMs that you specify. Google lists disaster recovery as a use for reservations. You pay for the reserved resources at the on-demand rate while the reservation exists.

whyWrong.A: The project already has enough quota. More quota does not make zonal capacity available.
whyWrong.B: A compute flexible commitment lowers the price of eligible usage. It does not support attached reservations, so it gives no assured capacity.
whyWrong.C: A MIG that scales out from 0 VMs still needs zonal capacity at failover time. Autohealing recreates VMs that fail their health check, but it does not reserve capacity.

stem: An online travel company runs three service layers on GKE: a web frontend, a booking API, and an inventory service that uses Cloud SQL. Each layer retries a failed call 3 times with no wait. During a short Cloud SQL failover, the database received many times its normal request rate, and the recovery took 40 minutes instead of 2. The team wants the Google-recommended fix for the cause of the slow recovery. What should you recommend?

options.text: Keep 3 retries at each layer, and add a fixed 1-second wait between the attempts.
Retry at one layer only, with a retry limit and randomized exponential backoff.
Add exponential backoff without jitter at each layer, so that retries follow a fixed schedule.
Increase the Cloud SQL machine size and connection limit to absorb the retry traffic.

explanation: Retries at every layer multiply. Four attempts at each of three layers can create 64 attempts on the database for one user action. The SRE book recommends that you retry at one level only, limit the retries for each request, and always use randomized exponential backoff. Without randomness, a small outage causes retries that arrive at the same time and amplify the overload.

whyWrong.A: A fixed wait keeps the retries of all clients in step, so they arrive in waves. The layers still multiply the attempts.
whyWrong.C: Without jitter, the retries from many clients arrive at the same time. Retries at each layer still multiply the load.
whyWrong.D: A larger database costs more and leaves the cause in place, because the layers still multiply the retries.

sources.title: Addressing Cascading Failures (SRE book)
sources.evidence: avoid amplifying retries by issuing retries at multiple levels: a single request at the highest layer may produce a number of attempts as large as the product of the number of attempts at each layer

sources.title: Addressing Cascading Failures (SRE book)
sources.evidence: If retries aren't randomly distributed over the retry window, a small perturbation (e.g., a network blip) can cause retry ripples to schedule at the same time, which can then amplify themselves

stem: A media company expects 10 times its normal traffic on a Cloud Run service during a live event. The team plans a load test. The draft plan publishes messages to a Pub/Sub push subscription that targets the service. It judges success from the `request_count` and latency charts of the service in Cloud Monitoring. Which two changes should you recommend? (Choose two.)

options.text: Generate the load with a test harness, such as JMeter, that controls the request rate and the concurrency.
Set the maximum instances of the service to 1 during the test, so that each test run gives the same result.
Keep Pub/Sub as the load source, and raise the publish rate until the service starts to return errors.
Measure the latency and the errors at the load generator, and compare them with the server-side charts.
Generate the load with Cloud Monitoring uptime checks that send requests from all regions each minute.

explanation: Google recommends a test harness, such as JMeter, because you must control the rate and the concurrency to know what you test. Pub/Sub cannot control the rate of the traffic or the number of clients. Also measure the results at the client. The Cloud Run `request_count` metric excludes requests that do not reach an instance, such as requests that fail at the maximum number of instances. So the server charts can look healthy during an overload.

whyWrong.B: One instance stops the service from scaling out, so the test cannot show whether the service scales out linearly with the load.
whyWrong.C: Pub/Sub cannot control the rate of the traffic or the number of clients, so the team does not know what load it tests.
whyWrong.E: Uptime checks send a small number of periodic requests to check availability. They cannot generate a controlled high load.

sources.title: Load testing best practices
sources.evidence: Pub/Sub is a poor choice of tool to generate load because you cannot control the rate of the traffic and number of clients.

sources.title: Load testing best practices
sources.evidence: You can query logs captured by JMeter, where the logs include latencies measured at the client.

sources.title: Google Cloud metrics: P through Z
sources.evidence: Excludes requests that are not reaching your container instances (for example, unauthorized requests or when maximum number of instances is reached).

stem: A company serves a stateless web app from a regional MIG behind a global external Application Load Balancer. The MIG has 6 VMs, 2 in each of three zones. Load tests show that the app needs 6 VMs at peak. Each new VM needs 12 minutes to warm up before it can serve. In a zone failure drill at peak, latency and errors rose until the zone came back. You must survive the loss of one zone at peak at the lowest cost. What should you do?

options.text: Enable autohealing with an application health check, so that the MIG recreates the VMs of the failed zone.
Enable autoscaling on CPU utilization with a 12-minute initialization period and a minimum of 6 VMs.
Increase the target size of the MIG to 9 VMs, so that two zones can carry the peak traffic alone.
Add a second regional MIG with 6 VMs in another region as a second backend of the load balancer.

explanation: Google recommends that you overprovision a regional MIG in three zones by at least 50%. With 9 VMs, 3 in each zone, the two remaining zones still run 6 VMs when one zone fails. After a zone failure, the MIG adds no VMs in the other zones unless autoscaling is on. Autoscaling is too slow here, because each new VM needs 12 minutes before it can serve.

whyWrong.A: During a zone failure, the MIG does not add VMs in the remaining zones unless autoscaling is on. Autohealing does not restore the lost capacity.
whyWrong.B: New VMs need 12 minutes before they can serve, so users see errors for the first minutes of a zone failure at peak.
whyWrong.D: A second region runs 12 VMs, or 200% of the need. It protects against more failures, but it costs more than the 9 VMs that one zone loss requires.

sources.title: About regional MIGs
sources.evidence: By overprovisioning to 150%, you can ensure that if 1/3 of the capacity is lost, 100% of traffic is supported by the remaining zones.

sources.title: About regional MIGs
sources.evidence: The number of instances that are part of the regional MIG in the remaining zones continue to serve traffic. No new instances are added and no instances are redistributed (unless you set up autoscaling).
